en: Became chief of a people bound by kinship;
Born a daughter, Kardygach
Shook the peoples of the world.
Of that fierce, unbridled woman,
Let me tell the lion-like courage.
When the massed Chinese, the khakan's people,
From beneath Kardygach herself
They shot Telkyzyl,
When Beijing's people raised an uproar
And closed a circle round her,
The stars in heaven were eclipsed.
Riding openly into the fight,
Khan Saikal, daughter of Karacha,
Clothed her in armor no shot could pierce,
Mounted her upon Teltoru.
When they crossed Ala-Aigyr,
The two raced for their lives;
When they fled this way,
Almambet, son of Azyz Khan,
Hero Chubak, son of Akbaltai,
The two khans, Ajybai and Bakai,
And Manas Khan's forty zaisans,
Who rejoiced at the word of an enemy,
Whose tiger valor was manifest,
Who drank poison when told to drink water,
Who spilled entrails when told to spill blood,
Who cut off heads when told to take caps—
Manas Khan's forty wolves—
When the two maidens made their escape,
Went out scouting and met them.
The stars streamed down from heaven.
Through their courage, the two maidens
Came safe and sound, just so,
And met the forty champions.
Seeing the aspect of those forty champions,
The pursuers lost their wits:
The Chinese who pursued the maidens,
And their mighty Kalcha Kongurbai,
Turned and fled in their pursuit.
God had granted it thus.
The deeds of courage done by the maidens,
My dear Bakai and Almambet
Had clearly witnessed themselves.
Saikal, daughter of Karacha,
Of the Kyrgyz people whose battle-cry is Oigut,
They gave back to her father, Karacha Khan.
Kardygach, daughter of Jakyp Khan,
At Zhelpinish, the end of the earth,
To Jarmanas of the wicked people—
They gave her to Jarmanas.
Many months passed after months,
Many days passed after days.
No sight of her could be caught;
No tidings came to be told.
No swift tulpar crossed between them;
Not one human soul came or went.
She had become far distant.
This year I hear from travelers
Who came from Zhelpinish itself:
Sarybai, son of the ogre,
Against Jarmanas and Kardygach
Came out to joust, I hear.
All the wicked people
He struck down with his spear, I heard.
He battered the wicked people
And made them destitute, I heard.
Leaving no maned mare for them to ride,
No fat-tailed lamb for them to eat,
He chased and drove them out, I heard.
Your devastating aunt Kardygach
Stood exchanging mounted blows,
Riding sixty coursers to death,
Fighting six months without respite.
Unable to overcome him, Kardygach,
In her battle against Sarybai,
All her treasury,
Wasting it upon the open ground,
Scattered and abandoned, I heard.
Abandoning her great people,
Starting tumultuous battle and strife,
Saying, 'I shall go to my brother, Manas Khan;
I shall bring my Manas back with me,
And on Sarybai, son of the ogre,
Then I shall take my revenge,'
She traveled six months without rest,
Hurrying and hastening over a great distance,
Saying, 'I shall go to Manas,'
And must have reached the Talas.
There was no croaking raven,
No cawing crow;
She must have found no people.
She must have seen the empty land.
Unable to learn whether he was dead
Or whether he was alive,
Your aunt, this very year,
Seven days after her arrival,
Must have found no place to settle.
To inquire and learn fully,
She must have found no people.
If you should encounter her,
Your elder, the leopard Bakai Khan,
Is the hero who will find a way,
The lion who will tell her tactfully.
Your aunt is a fierce warrior woman;
Lest she harm you without recognizing you,
Orphan, take care of that.
Such is your aunt's condition.
Let me leave this here.
Again, my son, hear my words;
Let me begin with what lies nearer.
There are assembled beys;
If you go farther up,
There are the houses of your uncles, the six villains.
He will teach you what you do not know,
The learned saint Bakai,
And lead you in to that utterly ignorant dog Köbösh.
When you enter, your uncle
Will swell with fury;
The pig's wineskin-sized nose will spread.
Akylai, daughter of Shooruk,
That short-witted creature too,
Was your father Sultan Manas's
Wife whom he had taken by force.
She was his senior wife.
The people know her dog-like ways;
She has married that dog Köbösh,
Has become his senior wife,
And over property, wealth, and treasure
Has become the mistress.
When you enter the palace,
Akkelte, left by your father Manas,
Is the treasure for you to fire,
The keen weapon left by your father Manas.
When one slings the blessed thing upon oneself,
It is the mirror of one's shoulder;
When aimed at a battling enemy,
It is the comfort of one's borrowed life.
With gaping mouth and apple-shaped head,
When one's borrowed life is hard pressed,
When enemies besiege one from afar,
It will not fail for sixty days,
Making no distinction between near and far.
Let me tell of Akkelte:
Your father was born in Altai;
He clashed with unbelievers.
When he reached twelve years of age,
Against the Black Chinese and Manchu people,
The Black Kalmyks and Solon people
He did battle; from Altai,
To see the Muslim people
Your heroic father longed,
To find a way to reach Talas,
To see the faces of Muslims,
And the countless livestock taken as booty from the Chinese
To the needy, the wretched poor,
To give as spoils.
With these wishes your father,
Not taking a month's respite,
Fought month after month.
With Khan Joloi of the Kalmyks
He exchanged battle-cries.
The stars in heaven were eclipsed;
He wrought a slaughter in plain sight.
He found a land like Talas;
He found the Argyn and Kyrgyz people.
When he had reached twelve years,
When God granted his wish,
When your father came to Talas,
When he saw the road to Mediyan,
His courage roused him to fervor.
Hero Bakai, son of Oluyat,
Met your father the khan.
They chewed white wheat flour together,
To go to war together,
To bring calamity upon their foes,
To remain inseparable.
They chewed white wheat flour together,
Clasping the Holy Quran.
The stars in heaven stirred;
They became friends into the world beyond.
Like white wheat flour
They were kneaded into one.
Like the hair of a white saiga
They became close, heartfelt friends.
Like a stream flowing from the foothills
They flowed swiftly together.
The Magnanimous One and hero Bakai
Joined together thus.
The tale of the tiger, dauntless Bakai,
Made your father rejoice.
Sultan Bakai, favored by Khidr,
Melted souls with his conduct.
Every word he told
Your noble father Manas
Moved his soul to deep sorrow.
His deeds delighted the soul.
He had drawn a line there;
There upon the open ground, Bakai,
To your father Sultan Manas,
Told a wondrous tale:
'Devastating Manas, hear my words.
I kept pondering within myself;
One day I saw in a dream
That I had mounted a spirit horse.
I climbed Kara-Too,
And the four corners of the world
I surveyed thoroughly.
Long I wandered in sorrow.
Khan Manas, tall as a mountain,
If the one God so ordained, you yourself,
I wondered whether I would ever see.
Zhelpinish, at the end of the earth,
Became my heart's craving;
For seven years I searched there.
In Jerusalem, Baghdad, and Egypt
I searched in weary desperation.
I spent nights at holy shrines;
My hero, I prayed to the one Allah for you.
Saying, “The leopard Manas will come;
Somehow my eyes will see him.
Like the moon risen overhead,
My guiding sign will come this year;
The dark, dauntless lion,
My companion will come this year.”
I oppressed the people of Crimea,
Imposing levies on its people,
Laying burdens upon its land,
Demanding, “Find me fine steel!”
They put all their skill to work;
Sixty smiths gathered,
All distinguished masters.
Only after six months did they find the way
And make Akkelte.
Upon the slope of Kaiyp-Kyr,
At the edge of the frontier,
I wrapped it in folded silk,
Entrusting it to my dear hero Manas.
When I slaughtered an offering to Bahauddin,
Into a cave for safekeeping
I placed it as a deposit.
They struck together at my very roots:
My belongings, the whole of them,
The Russians stole away.
Let us take that gun back.
If they will not heed our words,
If they will not give that gun,
Let us fight six months, five months,
Until we are utterly spent.'
At the edge of an empty plain,
Along the face of the pine forest,
On a yellow plain like the moon,
Riding their bay mares,
Wearing their yellow coats,
All of them riding bareback,
Sixty Russian land surveyors
Came out upon the plain.
